en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 51.
The Training Rule on Drinking Liquor:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Cetiya people, proceeded toward Bhaddavatikā.
The cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, they said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One not go to Ambatittha.
At Ambatittha, venerable sir, there dwells in the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic a nāga who possesses psychic power, is venomous, and has a terrible poison.”

“Do not harass the Blessed One. When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent. A second time also... [as before]... he remained silent. A third time also... [as before]... he remained silent. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One accept the meal; let the Sublime One accept the meal. Today is the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day, with its clear moon. It would be fitting for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have assembled for the Uposatha. When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent. A fourth time also, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One accept the meal; let the Sublime One accept the meal. Today is the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day, with its clear moon. It would be fitting for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have assembled for the Uposatha. When this was said, the Blessed One accepted the meal by remaining silent. Then the Venerable Ānanda, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance by his silence, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda had hard and soft food prepared at his own residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, venerable sir; the meal is ready. Then, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and went together with a number of bhikkhus to the residence of the Venerable Ānanda, where he sat down on the appointed seat. Then the Venerable Ānanda, with his own hand, served and satisfied the Blessed One with the hard and soft food. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the Venerable Ānanda took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, today is the fifteenth day, the Uposatha day, with its clear moon. It would be fitting for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who have assembled for the Uposatha. A third time, the cowherds, shepherds, and farmers who were traveling along said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One not go to Ambatittha.
At Ambatittha, venerable sir, there dwells in the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic a nāga, powerful and possessing a terrible venom."
"Therefore, do not harass the Blessed One.
For a third time, the Blessed One remained silent.
Then, as the Blessed One was traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived at Bhaddavatikā. There, indeed, the Blessed One stayed at Bhaddavatikā.
Then the Venerable Sāgata approached the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic of Ambatittha; having approached,
he entered the fire-hall, prepared a grass mat, and sat down with his legs crossed,
holding his body erect and establishing mindfulness before him.
That nāga saw the Venerable Sāgata having entered. Upon seeing him, he became dejected and emitted smoke;
the Venerable Sāgata also emitted smoke.
Then that nāga, unable to endure the insult, burst into flames.
The Venerable Sāgata also entered the fire-element and blazed up.
Then the Venerable Sāgata, having exhausted the serpent’s fiery power with his own fiery power, approached Bhaddavatikā.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Bhaddavatikā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Kosambī.
The lay followers of Kosambī heard: “It is said that the Venerable Sāgata has engaged in combat with the Ambatitthika Nāga.
Then, as the Blessed One was traveling by stages on his journey, he arrived at Kosambī. Thereupon, the lay followers of Kosambī went out to meet the Blessed One and approached the Venerable Sāgata;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Sāgata, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, the lay followers of Kosambī said this to the Venerable Sāgata:
“Venerable sir, what is rare and pleasing for the masters? What should we prepare?

When this was said, the group-of-six monks said to the lay followers of Kosambī: “Friends, there is a kind of fermented drink called *kāpotikā* which is rare and pleasing to the monks; you should prepare that.
Then the lay followers of Kosambī, having prepared *kāpotikā* fermented drink in every house, [approached] the Venerable...
Seeing Venerable Sāgata having entered for alms, they said this to him:
“Drink, venerable sir, the pigeon-colored gruel; drink, venerable sir, the pigeon-colored gruel!
Then Venerable Sāgata, having drunk the pigeon-colored gruel at every house, fell down at the city gate as he was leaving the city.
Then the Blessed One, while departing from the city together with a large number of bhikkhus, saw the Venerable Sāgata lying prostrate at the city gate.
Seeing him, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, take hold of Sāgata.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Having taken the Venerable Sāgata to the monastery, they laid him down with his head toward the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Sāgata turned over, placing his feet toward the Blessed One, and lay down.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, was Sāgata not formerly respectful and deferential toward the Tathāgata?
“Yes, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, does Sāgata now have respect and reverence for the Tathāgata?
“No, Bhante.
“Did Sāgata not, bhikkhus, engage in combat with the Nāga Ambatitthika?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But now, monks, is Sāgata able to engage in combat with a nāga?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Monks, would that which, having been drunk, would cause one to lose consciousness, be something fit to be drunk?
“No, indeed, venerable sir.
“Monks, for Sāgata, that was unbecoming, unsuitable, unworthy, unbecoming of a recluse, improper, and not to be done.”
"How indeed, monks, could Sāgata drink liquor?
This, monks, would not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Regarding the drinking of fermented liquor and spirits: it is an offense of expiation.
Herein, “fermented liquor” (surā) means liquor made from flour, liquor made from cakes, liquor made from boiled rice, or that which has had yeast added, being a mixture of various ingredients.

"Meraya" refers to a fermented liquor made from flowers, a fermented liquor made from fruits, a honey-based liquor, a molasses-based liquor, or one prepared from a combination of ingredients. "Should drink" means:
If one drinks even as much as the tip of a blade of kusa grass, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one drinks intoxicants with the perception that they are intoxicants, there is an offense of expiation.
If one drinks intoxicants while in doubt as to whether they are intoxicants, there is an offense of expiation.
If one drinks what is intoxicating while perceiving it as non-intoxicating, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives what is not intoxicating as intoxicating, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is in doubt regarding what is not intoxicating, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one perceives what is not intoxicant as not intoxicant.
There is no offense if it is not intoxicant but has the color, smell, and taste of intoxicant, and one drinks it.
In the preparation of soup,
the preparation of meat,
and the preparation of oil.
[It is] in the case of āmalaka-phāṇita,
drinking non-intoxicating ariṭṭha,
or one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The first training rule on drinking fermented liquor is finished.
